title: What Aristotle Can Teach America
author: Casey Chalk
summary: Casey Chalk uses Mark Blitz's book on Aristotle's political philosophy to argue that America's troubles lie less in policy and political opponents than in the character of its citizens. He notes that ordinary people have little power over big policy questions, yet civic participation and trust are low, and he asks whether the problem is internal. Drawing on Blitz, he explains that Aristotle tied happiness to ethical virtue and contemplation of the good, not to satisfying desires, so that virtue is foundational to political life. He argues that the American founders shared this view of liberty as an opportunity to achieve virtue, not as license, and that law and culture inevitably form character. He also flags Aristotle's caution about size, since friendship and statesmanship are harder in a nation of 330 million. He ends with Aristotle's claim that education of the young is the legislator's chief object, and a call for citizens to repent and improve before demanding that leaders change.
points: The essay locates national decline in citizens' character and civic habits rather than in distant parties or systems, which individuals have little power to change.
Aristotle's happiness is tied to ethical virtue, which is why virtue is foundational to politics and not merely private self-improvement.
The founders understood liberty as the opportunity to achieve virtue, and Blitz argues liberal democracy depends on modern virtues like responsibility, industriousness and civility.
Law and culture cannot be morally neutral because they necessarily form a certain character, so legislating morality is unavoidable.
Aristotle's view that the education of the young is the legislator's chief object implies that a better character is always the cause of a better regime.
quotes: What if the problem with America is not “out there” manifested in our political opponents or a rigged system, but internally, with us?

We moderns tend to think of it exclusively in reference to satisfying our desires, but the Greeks’ conception of the term focused on ethical virtue and contemplating the good; in other words, aligning our thoughts and actions with what is objectively good
Thus, virtue is not only some sort of stoic program of self-improvement but is foundational to the political life.
As many scholars of the American founding have argued, liberty was never intended by the founders as “license,” meaning the freedom to do anything. Instead, it gave the opportunity to achieve virtue.
As Blitz perceptively observes, for all of the talk of American government and law being dispassionate and neutral, it is impossible for both not to form a certain character.
It is for this reason that “legislating morality” is impossible to avoid, because all law is based in morality.
That should not be a controversial assertion: The more virtuous the nation, the more virtuous the regime.
Many of us are too proud (or self-righteous) to acknowledge that it is we who need to repent and improve as much as it is those who lead us.
